The latest SB Nation Reacts survey paints an increasingly bleak picture of fan sentiment surrounding the Indianapolis Colts, with just 19 percent of fans expressing confidence that the franchise is headed in the right direction. That's another significant decline from last week's 31 percent and a staggering 28-percentage-point drop from the 47 percent recorded just two weeks ago, shortly after the firing of general manager Chris Ballard.

Whatever optimism emerged following Ballard's dismissal appears to have disappeared almost as quickly as it arrived. The Colts have lost four consecutive games, falling to 2-6 following Sunday's humiliating 42-7 defeat against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Indianapolis was thoroughly outplayed in virtually every aspect of the game, trailing 28-0 at halftime before suffering its most lopsided loss of the season. With the offense continuing to struggle under Daniel Jones and the defense showing little consistency, there has been very little on the field to suggest that a turnaround is approaching.

The organization's recent roster overhaul has only added to the uncertainty. Indianapolis traded Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner last week, parting ways with two of its most accomplished veterans in exchange for future draft capital. While those decisions may ultimately benefit the franchise in the long run, they also signal that the Colts are increasingly focused on rebuilding rather than competing this season. With no first-round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft and several important roster questions still unanswered, fans understandably have concerns about how quickly the organization can return to contention.

The decline in confidence does not necessarily mean fans oppose the direction ownership has chosen, particularly given the frustration surrounding the previous regime. However, the results suggest that meaningful organizational changes alone have not been enough to restore faith in the franchise. Indianapolis still needs to demonstrate that it has a realistic plan for building a competitive roster, and the decisions made over the next several months could go a long way toward determining whether that confidence eventually returns.

Elsewhere in this week's survey, fans were asked whether the Colts should trade star running back Jonathan Taylor ahead of the November 10 deadline, and the results were surprisingly decisive. An overwhelming 73 percent of respondents supported moving Taylor, despite the 27-year-old remaining one of the NFL's premier running backs and arguably the most important player on Indianapolis' offense.

The results reflect just how much the conversation surrounding the Colts has changed over the past several weeks. Taylor remains an elite offensive weapon and is under contract through 2028, but with Indianapolis potentially several years away from seriously competing again, there is a legitimate question about whether his remaining prime seasons align with the organization's rebuilding timeline. Multiple contenders have reportedly expressed interest, and with the Colts believed to be seeking a first-round selection or a comparable package, moving Taylor could provide valuable draft capital for whoever takes over as general manager.

There is still a strong argument for keeping him, particularly with the Colts already lacking established offensive weapons and potentially facing another quarterback change in the coming years. Taylor has also maintained that he wants to win in Indianapolis and has not requested a trade, making his situation different from some of the other players reportedly seeking opportunities elsewhere.

Nevertheless, the survey results suggest that a substantial majority of participating Colts fans would support another major trade if it helps accelerate the franchise's rebuilding process. Whether Indianapolis ultimately receives an offer compelling enough to move Taylor remains to be seen, but with the deadline rapidly approaching, the organization faces another decision that could significantly shape its future.

#2794. The best version of Devin Booker is the one attacking early

Sometimes all it takes is a spark, however small, to start a fire and change a team's trajectory. Even if that spark comes against an opponent you wouldn't necessarily consider quality.

The Phoenix Suns' 117-104 victory over the Orlando Magic might be that spark, although with Houston and San Antonio staring them down on the schedule over the next few days, there's a chance we won't look back at this game as the moment that ignited some great blaze. But there were things we witnessed that can be deposited into the old adjustments bank, lessons that could serve as valuable reference points when trying to manufacture future victories.

One of those lessons, as obvious as it might seem, is that feeding Devin Booker early remains one of the best ways to give this team an opportunity to win basketball games.

Booker is the $57 million man, and constructing a roster that forces him to assume duplicative responsibilities within the starting lineup isn't exactly ideal. Too often, we see Booker drift away from his natural role as a shooting guard and become the primary playmaker, tasked with creating opportunities for everyone else rather than focusing on what he does best.

Against Orlando, we saw something different. In the first half, Booker went 8-of-13 from the field, including 3-of-4 from beyond the arc and a perfect 4-of-4 from the free-throw line, scoring 23 points while establishing himself as the focal point of the offense.

Granted, this was the Orlando Magic. Quality opponents have demonstrated the ability to scheme Booker out of games, as we saw earlier this season against a shorthanded Oklahoma City Thunder team. And that's precisely why the argument for having a quality facilitator persists.

When you have somebody capable of assuming the responsibility of distributing the basketball, opposing defenses have another variable to account for. They have to dedicate attention to disrupting that player's ability to initiate the offense, which can create more opportunities for Booker to operate as a scorer. And when Booker gets going early, it creates opportunities for everyone around him. As he begins to command the defensive gravity we know he possesses, teammates find themselves with more space and cleaner looks. The hope is that by the time an opposing defense figures out how to slow him down, Booker has already inflicted enough damage to force them into scrambling, opening up opportunities for the rest of the roster to capitalize.

Getting Devin Booker engaged early should be the North Star for this team. If opposing defenses are finding ways to take the ball out of his hands, then it's the coaching staff's responsibility to scheme ways to get it back into his hands in situations where he can be effective.

Here's a fun stat for you. Throughout his career, Booker has attempted 13 or more field goals in the first half of a game 110 times. In those games, the Suns have a .582 winning percentage. And when Booker does what he did last night, shooting 60% or better from the field while attempting at least 13 shots in the first half, that winning percentage climbs to .727. What's interesting is that since the acquisition of Bradley Beal prior to the 2023-24 season, Booker has attempted 13 or more field goals in the first half 30 times. The other 80 times occurred pre-Beal, with 46 occurring alongside Chris Paul.

I'm certainly not breaking any new ground by suggesting that your most skilled scorer should be looking to score early and often, especially when doing so creates opportunities for the players around him. But that's exactly what we witnessed against Orlando. Booker scored only seven points in the second half, yet he added four assists as Dillon Brooks and Miles Bridges began finding more opportunities to contribute offensively, benefiting from the defensive gravity Booker had established earlier in the game.

Perhaps this needs to become a point of emphasis for the coaching staff, along with a mental adjustment for Booker himself. Because when you look at the rosters he's played alongside since Chris Paul left town, it's difficult to argue that they've consistently been constructed to maximize his greatest strength, which can create a malaise and affinity for falling into distribution responsibilities rather than getting yours.

Playing alongside Bradley Beal, whose availability was frequently compromised by injuries, eventually led to stretches in which Eric Gordon or Tyus Jones ran the offense. Now Booker finds himself sharing the backcourt with Jalen Green, another player whose natural instincts lean toward scoring rather than facilitating. None of those combinations has been particularly conducive to allowing Booker to operate consistently in the role where he's most dangerous.

While there are legitimate criticisms of Booker's game, particularly his struggles executing in clutch situations and the difficulties he encounters when more physical defenders impose their will on him, those concerns shouldn't prevent us from recognizing what he does well. When Booker establishes himself offensively early, forces defenses to react, and creates opportunities for his teammates to capitalize, that's the version of Devin Booker this team needs. And when that approach contributes to a much-needed victory, it deserves recognition and applause.

The Suns aren't going to solve every roster deficiency overnight, and the challenges of getting Booker quality looks against better competition aren't going anywhere. But there's something to be said for simplifying the approach and putting your best player in positions to succeed. Orlando provided a reminder of what happens when Booker dictates the offense rather than reacting to it. If Phoenix is searching for a spark that can become something sustainable, getting Booker going early seems like a pretty damn good place to start.

#2789. Report: Warriors contact Bulls, Pelicans, and Bucks about Kristaps Porzingis trade

The Golden State Warriors have contacted the New Orleans Pelicans, Chicago Bulls, and Milwaukee Bucks to gauge the organization's interest in a potential trade for center Kristaps Porzingis (or really his contract), per a report by Brett Siegel of ClutchPoints. With Porzingis likely headed for retirement and accepting the Warriors withholding his salary, Siegel reports that he is expected to accept a significant buyout from his $20 million salary. The Dubs front office is trying to use his contract as a trade exception in the next month to solidify the team's depth without limiting their options at the trade deadline.

"Among the many teams the Warriors have contacted since the start of the season, as reported earlier on Friday in our weekly newsletter, ClutchPoints has been able to confirm with league sources three teams in particular: the Milwaukee Bucks, Chicago Bulls, and New Orleans Pelicans," Siegel wrote.

The Warriors interest in Pelicans wings Trey Murphy III and Herb Jones has been reported on for years, and the Dubs reportedly called New Orleans about center Yves Missi earlier this season as well. However, the fact that the two sides have not previously agreed to a deal should leave fans skeptical that a deal will happen now (especially months before the trade deadline).

Siegel's reporting suggests the Warriors and Bucks were not close to a deal for Myles Turner, with different evaluations of his contract's value. As for the Bulls, Siegel highlighted center Jalen Smith.

"Going back to the topic of potential trade suitors for Porzingis, the Warriors showed interest in Bulls' center Jalen Smith in a potential Porzingis-oriented deal with Chicago, but the Bulls have not shown a willingness to make such a move at this time, sources said," Siegel said. "The Bulls are wanting to evaluate their roster and potential moves closer to the trade deadline unless draft compensation is included, despite opening the year as one of the worst teams in the NBA."

Smith would be an excellent to the Warriors current front court depth. While he lacks the explosive ceiling that Golden State hoped to get from Porzingis, he is an incredibly well rounded role player who would give head coach Steve Kerr another center who can shoot threes other than 40-year old Al Horford.

The 10th overall pick in the 2020 NBA Draft by the Phoenix Suns, Smith never found his footing in Phoenix and was quickly viewed around the league as a bust before finding consistency with the Indiana Pacers. Over the past five seasons, split between Indiana and Chicago, Smith has averaged 9.4 points, 5.9 rebounds, and 0.8 blocks on 50.1%/34.3%/74.9% shooting in 18.0 minutes per game (254 games, 76 starts).

Still only 26, Smith has been the primary starting center for the first time in his career this season. While he is posting career highs in minutes (22.5), points (11.0), rebounds (7.8), assists (1.8), and blocks (0.9) per game so far this season, the Bulls are 1-7 and have been among the worst teams in the league. Slated to be a free agent at the end of the season, Smith seems destined to be traded before the deadline for a package built around second-round picks. The question is, will the Warriors be able to convince the Bulls to make that move before the new year?

The Warriors only have two tradeable second round picks, one in 2030 and another in 2033. One added enticement they could add to a deal with the Bulls, who have notoriously cheap owner Jerry Reinsdorf, would be to take back either Buddy Hield or Zach Collins alongside Smith. The Warriors would likely waive either player, but would effectively be taking $18-$19 million off the Bulls books. Assuming the Bulls agreed to a buyout with Porzingis in the $6-8 million range that Siegel speculates, Bulls ownership could save around $10 million.

#2788. Brandon Aiyuk plans to meet with 49ers at team's business offices, not team facility

49ers tight end George Kittle was right, sort of. Receiver Brandon Aiyuk won't "get in" the team facility on Friday, because he's not trying to.

Per agent Drew Rosenhaus, Friday's meeting will happen at the team's business offices and not at the team's practice facility.

That makes the session not a formal reporting-for-duty by Aiyuk, in the hopes of forcing the team's hand. As explained earlier today, the NFL still hasn't reinstated Aiyuk from the reserve/left squad list — even though Rosenhaus filed the request on October 27.

Instead, it's a meeting presumably aimed at negotiating a resolution to the situation.

The 49ers pushed to reporters on Thursday night the idea that Aiyuk's return to the NFL is tied to the $13 million the team believes he owes in previously paid signing bonus. That shouldn't be part of the analysis as to whether he's reinstated by the league, whether the 49ers put him on the roster again, and/or whether the 49ers cut him.

But they're making it an issue, because they can tie his ability to play to his willingness to wire the disputed funds to the team.

So that's what's happening. The brakes already have been applied to what should have been an administrative and automatic process. The league and the 49ers are working together to help the team get money back from Aiyuk before Aiyuk is permitted to get back into the league.

Then there's the fact that an active arrest warrant is pending for Aiyuk, arising from a speeding incident. The business meeting could potentially be interrupted by an attempt to enforce a specific item of police business.

#2786. Steph Curry’s viral Klay Thompson exchange comes with bittersweet retirement admission

It's still strange for Golden State Warriors fans to see Klay Thompson wearing another team's jersey.

They had to do so once again on Thursday, when Thompson's Miami Heat came to town.

At least Steph Curry (who had 29 points in the Warriors- 120-100 win) managed to make light of this at one point in the game, when he pointed at his former teammate and gave a thumbs-up during a brief pause in the action.

Steph Curry pointing at Klay Thompson when the Golden State Warriors played the Miami Heat on Thursday. (@NBA).

A clip of Steph doing so went viral on social media, tallying over three million views since the NBA's X account posted it on Thursday night.

Even though Thompson (who didn't see what Curry did) didn't look too enthused during the viral clip, comments he made about reuniting with Curry postgame show how heartwarming it was for him.

"It was fun. It was really fun. He's still super crafty still to this day," Thompson, who had 11 points in the loss but blocked one of Curry's shots at one point, said.

Klay Thompson looking at at fan after Steph Curry pointed at him. (X/@NBA).

"What Steph is doing, I got to see it every night and it became normal, but to see it as an opponent it was incredible, especially that he's nearing 40 and he moves like a young athlete. It's all the respect in the world for him. He deserves all the accolades and adulation and money. He's just 1 of 1 and the game is going to miss him when he does hang it up," he added, per Yahoo Sports.

Thompson wasn't the only Splash Brother to allude to their respective careers reaching their twilight last night.

Stephen Curry #30 of the Golden State Warriors looks on during a game against the Miami Heat at Chase Center in San Francisco, California, Nov. 5, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

"It's definitely surreal, but it's also a blessing we're still playing. Every time we play against him it's one closer to the end. Just trying to appreciate it," Curry said to NBA TV after the game.

It's awesome for fans to see these two relishing what's left of their time on the court together, even when they're playing for different teams.

#2782. Former Steeler Explains Why Team Won’t End Up Trading For WR at Deadline

A former member of the Pittsburgh Steelers doesn't think the team will land another playmaker at the trade deadline.

There is a strong belief that the Pittsburgh Steelers will acquire another wide receiver before Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET trade deadline. However, former Steelers offensive lineman Trai Essex does not think that will eventually be the case.

Essex believes the Steelers will ultimately forego trading for another playmaker with wide receiver Roman Wilson on the cusp of returning from his injury.

"I'm a big Brian Thomas Jr. fan, and what he did his rookie year was fantastic in Jacksonville," Essex said on his Snap Count podcast. "But as we stand right now, do you think we need to trade for him? Because I think Roman is the key to all of this. I think if Roman comes back healthy, he is our man beater, and this is the defense we're getting a lot of because of the fact that DK [Metcalf] can't get off man coverage consistently. When Roman comes back, I think because of that, we don't trade for a wide receiver."

Wilson's return could provide a nice boost for the Steelers offense, but it still wouldn't hurt for the team to add another wide receiver to their room for the right price.

Metcalf has not lived up to expectations and wide receiver Michael Pittman Jr. looks to still be on injured reserve for the foreseeable future.

Not to mention, Wilson hasn't been so good that it should prevent the Steelers from trying to upgrade the position.

Since being selected in the third round of the 2024 NFL Draft, Wilson has only recorded 26 catches for 354 yards and four touchdowns while battling several injuries.

Pittsburgh Steelers wide receiver Roman Wilson during a preseason game against the New York Jets on Aug. 21, 2026. — Ed Thompson / Steelers Now

Meanwhile, there are several interesting names being thrown around as potential trade candidates, including Thomas and Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Josh Downs.

#2781. Westchester Knicks 2026-27 Season Primer

New York's G League affiliate opens its 2026-27 season tonight against the Maine Celtics in the Tip-Off Tournament. The roster features three players on two-way contracts, a returning fan favorite (hint: he's great on toast), and a collection of prospects hoping to dribble their way up to an NBA court.

With the Knicks operating near the second apron, Westchester provides a way to develop young players without committing additional standard roster spots. Two-way players can spend most of the season in White Plains while remaining available for NBA duty, subject to a limit of up to 50 games on the active roster. The G League has also given players like Deuce McBride and Tyler Kolek opportunities to get more work. Here's a peek at the players worth watching.

Of everyone on Westchester's roster, Dalton Knecht has the clearest path to helping the big club this season. The 2024 first-round pick (17th overall) arrived after the Lakers waived him, with New York releasing Kevin McCullar Jr. to make room for Knecht on a two-way contract. This low-risk move could pay off if the former Tennessee star rediscovers his shooting touch and improves his court awareness, which was a criticism raised in the comments section at Silver Screen and Roll.

The 25-year-old made a promising debut for the New York Knicks this week, scoring 10 points on efficient 4-of-6 shooting (including two threes) with seven boards, a dime, and a block in 16 minutes off the bench in a rout of the Bulls. Finding consistent playing time will be difficult, however. With Mikal Bridges, OG Anunoby, Josh Hart, Landry Shamet, Pacôme Dadiet, and Mohamed Diawara competing for minutes on the wings, Knecht will probably need an injury or another opening to receive an extended look. (TBH, he already looks ahead of Dadiet.)

Coach Mike Brown has said he'd rather see Knecht playing meaningful minutes in the G League than sitting on the NBA bench. Makes sense. Knecht needs opportunities to shoot, make decisions, and work through mistakes. He has shown he can score, but questions remain about his defense, shot selection, and ability to contribute consistently as a role player.

If Knecht performs well enough, the organization could eventually consider converting him to a standard NBA contract, which would require sufficient roster and financial room. For now, he should get plenty of opportunities to let it fly against G League competition.

Speaking of flamethrowers . . . Tyler "Silent K" Nickel might be the most straightforward fit for what the Knicks need. New York selected the Vanderbilt sharpshooter with the 47th pick in the 2026 NBA Draft after an impressive senior season. He followed that with a promising Summer League showing and signed a two-way contract.

From what we've seen, Nickel moves well without the ball, finds open space, and punishes defenses for leaving him unattended. The big league Knicks have several players capable of creating offense, and a dependable perimeter shooter who doesn't require many touches could fit nicely alongside them (see: Landry Shamet).

His defense will help determine how quickly the 23-year-old advances. He needs to prove he can handle quicker, stronger NBA bodies while maintaining his shooting efficiency against more aggressive closeouts. Westchester should give him plenty of reps to work on both.

Nickel doesn't seem to have Knecht's offensive versatility, but his shooting gives him a clearly defined role. If he can hold his own defensively, he could become a useful option for additional spacing. For the time being, Westchester might have its very own set of Splash Brothers to keep you entertained (at a reasonable price).

Jaden Akins took a less direct route to New York. Undrafted out of Michigan State in 2025, he spent last season with the Motor City Cruise after earning All-Big Ten third-team and All-Defensive recognition as a senior. His combination of scoring, secondary playmaking, and defense caught the Knicks' attention. Westchester acquired his returning player rights in September, and he secured a two-way contract before the season.

Akins faces considerable competition at the one- and two-guard spots. His best chance of separating himself is to use his time at Westchester to polish his defense and his work off the ball. Can he defend multiple positions, run an offense for stretches, and make open shots? Can he contribute consistently without committing unnecessary fouls or turnovers? Those qualities will probably matter more to New York than his individual scoring averages.

The fan favorite returns! Dink Pate returns to Westchester after a confusing offseason. The 6'8" wing, still only 20 years old, averaged approximately 16 points, seven rebounds, and four assists across 50 games with the club last season. He subsequently attempted to play college basketball at Providence, but that plan fell through amid questions about his NCAA eligibility. The Knicks signed and waived him on an Exhibit 10 contract, and he returned to Westchester, which already held his G League rights.

Pate has length, can create his own offense, and contributes as a rebounder and passer. His combination of physical tools and professional experience makes him one of Westchester's more interesting developmental players. Decision-making and efficiency are where he needs improvement.

Unlike Knecht, Nickel, and Akins, Pate doesn't have a two-way contract. He would need an available two-way or standard roster spot and a new NBA contract to join the big club. Westchester's rights also don't prevent another NBA team from signing him. Thus, his time in White Plains is a prove-it run for a broader audience—so we expect to see some inspired hooping from him this season.

Westchester's frontcourt includes several players who could provide useful depth. Liam Robbins, a seven-footer who went undrafted out of Vanderbilt in 2023, is probably the most recognizable. He showed some encouraging work around the iron during Summer League with the Knicks, and Westchester subsequently acquired his G League rights.

Robbins brings size, rebounding, and shot-blocking ability. The big league club could use more reliable center depth behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond, with James Wiseman slow to make an impression. Robbins could use his time in White Plains to convince the team he deserves a look—perhaps before the front office starts eyeing its surplus of guards as trade bait.

N'Faly Dante, the 6-foot-11 former Oregon center, is working his way back from an ACL injury. His size and athleticism lift our eyebrows, but getting healthy and regaining his previous form will be the immediate priorities.

Igor Miličić Jr., a 6-foot-10 forward out of Tennessee, brings international experience and positional versatility after spending time with the Delaware Blue Coats last season. Improving his outside shooting and defensive consistency would help him take the next step.

Westchester also has several forwards competing for rotation minutes. Nick Jourdain returns after averaging roughly eight points and more than five rebounds last season. The former Memphis forward provides rebounding, energy, and defensive effort. His journey from local tryout to returning player is a nice story, even if an NBA opportunity remains a longer shot.

Toby Okani, the former West Virginia wing, brings length and athleticism after spending time with multiple G League organizations. David Dixon, an undrafted forward out of Duquesne, and Tahj-Malik Campbell are also trying to establish roles after joining the training camp group.

Westchester's backcourt includes several capable players. Mitchell Mascari is worth watching after arriving from the Stockton Kings. The 6'5" guard shot approximately 42% from downtown last season, giving Westchester another option to stretch the floor.

Paul Zilinskas returns as a scoring option at guard and on the wing, while Amir "Primo" Spears joins the club after being selected 25th in the 2026 G League Draft. Spears brings extensive college experience, including a productive stint at UTSA, and spent last season playing professionally in Mexico.

The three two-way players will receive the most attention this season, although we'll also keep an eye on Pate ('cuz he's kinda electric). The rest of the roster will compete for minutes and try to establish themselves as dependable professional players. Westchester opens its Tip-Off Tournament schedule tonight at 7 p.m. against the Maine Celtics at the Portland Expo, then faces the same opponent at the same venue Sunday at 12:30 p.m. Both games will air on MSG Network.

#2778. ‘I’m really apolitical’: Jerry Jones claims he stays out of politics despite donating more than $1 million to Republicans

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones wants everyone to know that he doesn't take sides in politics. His recent donations tell a slightly different story.

Speaking on 105.3 The Fan on Friday, Jones described himself as "apolitical," saying that he can't afford to pick a party because the Cowboys have fans on both sides. That's an interesting claim from someone who poured more than $1 million into Republican causes ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.

On Friday, Jones was asked if he had reached out to any of Texas' newly elected officials, including Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, before they take office. He insisted his focus is on the Cowboys and nothing else.

"I'm really apolitical. I really can't afford to be a party because our fans are all parties. So, I'm very deliberate," Jones said, via The Dallas Morning News. "When I have something that will help the Cowboys, then I'm all in. And I'll go all out. But it's all about the Cowboys."

Jones said he has been told that he needs to be more socially involved, but that his priority is making the Cowboys entertaining.

"That's my 99 and nine-tenths percent reason for doing anything," he said. "That's what it is and getting really, intensely involved in [politics] is not my gig."

The Dallas Morning News' Joseph Hoyt was quick to point out that Jones donated to Paxton earlier this year.

Jones didn't stay out of politics for the entire interview, either. In the same appearance, he endorsed legalizing sports gambling in Texas and said he hoped that "the new turnover, you might say, in the politics will see it that way."

According to Front Office Sports, Jones gave $1 million to MAGA Inc., the super PAC aligned with President Donald Trump, during this election cycle. He also spent about $500,000 on Texas races, per FOS' Dennis Young and Margaret Fleming.

That included $250,000 to a joint fundraising committee for Ken Paxton, the Republican who lost Tuesday's Texas Senate race to Democrat James Talarico.

Jones' son, Cowboys executive vice president Jerry Jones Jr., also gave $50,000 to Sen. John Cornyn, whom Paxton beat in the Republican primary, and $100,000 to a PAC linked to Sen. Ted Cruz.

Jones hasn't only given to Republicans, though. Last month, the Jones family announced a $10 million gift to the Clinton Presidential Center in Little Rock – though it's worth noting that the donation is not a campaign donation or a political contribution. Instead, the money will go toward expanding and renovating the nonprofit presidential library. Jones and former President Bill Clinton are longtime friends who both grew up in Arkansas.

CHARLOTTE — Jordan Walsh isn't thrilled with his start to the season. The 22-year-old has played double-digit minutes in every game and has been tasked with guarding the opposing team's best players, as is customary.

But at Celtics shootaround Friday morning, Walsh said he was underwhelmed with his impact on the team so far.

"I think it's been okay," Walsh said. "I don't think it's been good or great or nothing like that. I think it's been just okay. Haven't been, like, the best version of myself, but the team's winning, everybody's happy, so it's all good."

Walsh started the first five games of the season but has come off the bench for the last three. He hasn't shot particularly well — he's shooting 38.2% from the field and 30% from three — but it's all in a very small sample. So far, he's averaging 4.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 15.4 minutes per night, both numbers slightly lower than last season.

"I haven't been playing great — but the starting, not starting thing, it's not about that," Walsh said. "That's just kind of like Joe's thing, like he wants to try new things. Like, that's fine. Walsh isn't on the court to stuff the stat sheet; his defensive success sometimes shows up as steals or blocks, but more often, it's more nuanced.

#2775. 6-2 Jaguars Facing Difficult Brian Thomas Balancing Act

With the NFL trade deadline arriving Tuesday, few Jacksonville Jaguars storylines carry as much league-wide attention as the future of wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. His diminished role since Week 4 has fueled a steady stream of speculation about what it means for his long-term place in Jacksonville, and the answer is slightly more complicated than simple usage charts suggest.

In a recent report, NFL Network's Cam Wolfe added some important context to the recent BTJ buzz. According to Wolfe, Thomas and Travis Hunter are close friends. Thomas is also well liked in the Jaguars' locker room, and his speed remains an asset even without the production to match. Wolfe also reported that the Jaguars have wondered whether last year's Tyson Campbell trade hurt their immediate locker room energy, and that the organization has "learned from it."

That last point deserves attention. After the Campbell trade to Cleveland in Week 6 of 2025, some players were reportedly unhappy with the move, and Jacksonville followed it with back-to-back tough losses to the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams. As is often the case in the NFL, winning will always cure the discomfort, however. The Jaguars closed out 2025 by going 9-1, and the locker room appeared no worse for wear. Still, it's easy to see how that experience could shape the team's approach to a third-year receiver this time around. However, it is hard to argue that the team made the wrong decision, based on the on-field outcomes, and their defensive scheme not matching the player. That's the key piece that makes this such a fascinating conversation. Where is the line between doing whatever is necessary to win versus doing what is needed for the locker room to be together?

The numbers, on the surface, show a player whose role has clearly shrunk considerably. Thomas currently ranks fourth on the team in targets (21), fifth on the team in receptions through eight games played (10), and seventh in yards (117) behind rookie Josh Cameron who has 123. Over his last four games combined, he has just one catch, a 12-yard touchdown against the Indianapolis Colts. On Thursday, he logged only 19 snaps against the Baltimore Ravens, a game in which he was relegated to the fourth receiver spot. However, that trend didn't start in Week 8. Thomas played a career-low 15 snaps against the Houston Texans in Week 6, before the Bye Week. After that game, head coach Liam Coen described the team's confidence in Thomas as a week-to-week matter and said simply, "Guys have to step up and make plays."

Ahead of the Colts game, Coen expressed faith that Thomas would continue helping the offense make plays. He quickly supported that faith, securing the opening-drive touchdown, his lone catch of the game.

Meanwhile, around the league, interest is as real as ever. ESPN's Dan Graziano reported that opposing teams are asking about Jacksonville's plans for Thomas and are expected to continue reaching out before the November 10 deadline. ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported that several executives believe Thomas's days in Jacksonville are numbered, and noted that a change of scenery could bring out the best in him. For a former 2024 Rookie of the Year finalist who topped 1,200 receiving yards as a rookie, that kind of interest is not surprising. What would be surprising is the team trading that caliber of player away for less than a first-round pick.

Thomas is not publicly asking to be traded. By all accounts, he's a hard worker and has embraced the team-first approach being built. But within Liam Coen's offense, his role appears to be that of the sacrificial X, stretching the defense vertically to open space underneath for the middle-of-the-field throws that drive the scheme. With Trevor Lawrence at his best working inside the hashes, that job rarely comes paired with a major statistical output. Jakobi Meyers, Parker Washington, Josh Cameron, and the Jacksonville tight end group all share that strength. Thomas doesn't, and that's okay. Thomas' role can be valuable to the offense without ever showing up in his stat line, which is an extremely difficult reality for a player of his pedigree.

Take the Baltimore matchup as an example: while Thomas was only on the field for 19 total snaps, he ran a route on 11 of Trevor Lawrence's 26 pass attempts (42.3%). Meanwhile, the team built up a 20-point third quarter lead in the rainy Baltimore night. On those 11 dropbacks, Lawrence was 6/11 (54.5%) for 109 yards, with four of the team's 11 passing first downs (36.4%), and the only passing touchdown – a 50 yarder to Parker Washington. The argument that BTJ pulls the primary coverage or opens up space could be supported.

This is a delicate situation. The Jaguars have spent two years shaping a finely tuned locker room, and they're looking to mold this roster into a legitimate Super Bowl contender. Trading away a well-liked player who is also a close friend of Hunter's carries risks that don't clearly show up on a stats sheet. For that reason, I expect Jacksonville to be buyers only at Tuesday's deadline.

Coen touched on the locker room impacts of prospective trades in his Friday media availability:

"How does it affect things moving forward, cap, future, other players, how we can resign or not, other guys, there's so much that goes into this time of the year. Also, being cognizant of the group that you have in the locker room and making sure that the guys all know in the building we're trying to do everything we can as an organization to make the best decisions for the group and for our team, because those guys are so important to what we're doing. It's a fine line. It's definitely a balancing act for sure, and everything that comes across your desk, you've got to make sure that you're looking at it through that lens; at least we are."

The one exception I could see would be a trading partner offering a corresponding move that makes sense for both sides, such as a deal that returns defensive tackle or safety talent, which effectively forces the team's hand in moving Thomas. With injuries already thinning the safety room, that kind of return is the only scenario where moving Thomas feels justified for a team with the roster Jacksonville has built.

#2772. Donovan Mitchell needs to shoot more, not less

If you've been online recently, you may have noticed that Donovan Mitchell has… pissed off a lot of Cleveland Cavaliers fans.

Twitter is ablaze with criticism. People want him traded. Some regret that he was ever traded for. Mitchell has become the crux of all problems; the shot-chucking 'dictator' who will never be the primary option on a championship team.

But everyone has it backwards; Donovan Mitchell needs to shoot more.

Mitchell's field goal attempts and usage rate are at career lows to start the year.

His assist percentage and shot chart are nearly identical to previous seasons.

That means Mitchell has less control over the offense than ever, despite some insisting that he's grown into a ball-dominant tyrant.

How did we get here? And why are fans feeling such a disconnect?

Mitchell has always been a scorer more than a passer. He currently ranks in the 41st percentile in assist-to-usage ratio — a stat that tracks how often a player is ending their possessions with an assist rather than a shot attempt or turnover.

This means that roughly half of the league's players are more likely to get an assist on any given possession than Donovan Mitchell. That can lead to games where it feels like Mitchell is hogging the ball while leaving his teammates hanging.

That gung-ho play style caused some frustration throughout last year's playoffs, and the complaints have carried into this year.

Fans want to know why Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen aren't getting the ball. Why do their leads disappear so often? And why haven't the Cavs gotten over the hump despite a roaring regular season?

Some have identified Mitchell's lack of playmaking as the problem.

Which, in fairness, is certainly a factor. Cleveland has lost big games in the past due to Mitchell's shot selection. He doesn't always make the right decision with the ball in his hands — and that can be difficult to watch as a fan.

But we should reframe this discussion. Let's start here.

Donovan Mitchell isn't a point guard. And maybe, he doesn't have to be.

Shai-Gilgeous Alexander was in the 29th percentile for assist-to-usage ratio when the Oklahoma City Thunder won the championship. He's in the 0th percentile now.

The truth is, championship-caliber players are allowed to have weak points. You are not disqualified if you can't do everything on your own.

Giannis Antetokounmpo never learned how to shoot. Nikola Jokic never became an elite defender. And the New York Knicks didn't win a championship last June because Jalen Brunson suddenly became an elite playmaker — they won because they delegated more playmaking responsibilities to Karl-Anthony Towns — leaving space for Brunson to do what Brunson does best… score the ball.

All of those teams identified their star's weakness, and built a roster around them that could insulate them.

The Cavs need a similar solution. They need someone who can take playmaking off of Mitchell's plate.

Darius Garland was the original fit. And, for a while, he would thread the needle beautifully. He sent the defense scattering into motion while Mitchell would catch the ball against a defense already on their back feet. That dynamic led to 64 wins — but unfortunately, Garland couldn't stay healthy.

James Harden was the next option. He's been more available than Garland, which was enough to help bolster the team to an Eastern Conference Finals run.

But Harden's style differs from Garland's. He's slower-paced, favoring a heliocentric style that inhibits stationary spacing around him. The result is fewer chances for Mitchell to attack in motion, nerfing his greatest strength as a slasher who can attack gaps.

All of this has culminated in the Cavs (and fans online) asking Mitchell to be more of a playmaker. But that is a fundamental misunderstanding of who he is — and how you win in the NBA by playing to your strengths.

I want to be clear that I am not advocating for Mitchell to go full Dion Waiters and ignore the other four Cavaliers sharing the court with him at any given time. He still needs to pass the ball — and he needs to choose the right moments to assert himself as a scorer.

You can't win by playing like a bull in a China shop. There has to be a delicate balance between scoring in bunches and releasing control of the offense to someone else. That's the key here.

Mitchell will never be a point guard. Any system that asks him to make reads at that level will learn the hard way. You can't force a square peg into a round hole.

You can, however, build a competitive team that understands who Mitchell is.

We know for a fact that Mitchell can go nuclear as a scorer in the playoffs. We've seen it multiple times.

But who can grab the reins and facilitate those high-scoring performances? Who is the Karl-Anthony Towns to his Jalen Brunson in this scenario?

The Cavs are still hoping that will be Harden. Additional support from Mobley would be welcomed. Whether that will be enough is certainly worth questioning.

But here's another cold, hard truth: Making it to the top of the mountain is hard. If we're being honest, it's damn near impossible. This franchise had the greatest player alive for 11 seasons and only made it to the finish line once.

Cleveland would need a myriad of miracles to win a championship with this group. Even if everything went right, they could still fall short. That's just the way it goes.

That's why sticking true to your identity is more important than anything. Being a bad version of someone else will always be inferior to being the best version of yourself.

I don't think Mitchell will lead Cleveland to a title through his playmaking. That feels like jumping the shark.

The Cavs do need him to be better defensively and to make better reads offensively, but that doesn't necessarily mean relinquishing his role as one of the highest-volume scorers in the league. That's who he is — that's who the team traded for.

Mitchell needs to be a world-class scorer. Nearly all of his attention on offense should be centered on getting his shot. Passing will always come second. Winning or losing comes down to Mitchell taking and making the big shots. That was the primary difference between him and Brunson last season.

Of course, any team would prefer a superstar who is capable of blending elite scoring with masterful playmaking and impactful defense. But, you work with what you have — and the Cavs have a dynamic scorer, not a floor general.

Accepting Mitchell's true nature and having the supporting cast insulate him with their playmaking is the most realistic path forward. It's the only path forward.

#2771. Minnesota-UCLA score predictions from Bring Me The Sports staff

The Gophers have a golden opportunity for their third field storming of the season this week when No. 8 UCLA comes to town. The Bruins are 8-0 this season and one of the best stories in the sport under first-year head coach Bob Chesney. Can Minnesota stop their momentum?

P.J. Fleck has a track record of performing well as a home underdog, and he has a great chance to add to that narrative this week against UCLA. The Bruins haven't played on the road since sneaking past Oregon for their best win on Oct. 10. The only thing that scares me for the Gophers' chances this week is a hangover after last week's emotional loss to Indiana, but I expect Fleck's team to be ready to end UCLA's perfect season.

I don't want to say UCLA doesn't deserve to be ranked in the top 10, but who have they actually beaten to prove they're legit? Oregon without Dante Moore? Please. Every team gives the Ducks a run for their money this year. Wisconsin's a fraud; Purdue can't play defense; Michigan State, Nevada, Maryland, San Diego State and Cal all stink. As long as Minnesota doesn't get gashed on the ground, they're going to limit Ty Dieffenbach through the air. Dieffenbach can't move (kinda like Mr. Statue Drake Lindsey), and that's bad news for the Bruins, who will go home with an 8-1 record

Since getting embarrassed by Purdue, the Gophers have upset Iowa and come oh-so-close to doing the same to Indiana. They've done it by dragging those ranked teams into low-scoring slugfests. Can they do it to undefeated UCLA this week? I'm inclined to think they can. Outside of Oregon and maybe Wisconsin, the Bruins haven't exactly beaten anyone notable. Backup QB Ty Dieffenbach is still fairly inexperienced. And UCLA is coming to Minneapolis to play in 40-degree temps in a game that kicks off at 9 a.m. Pacific time. This will be another big win and field storm for P.J. Fleck.

On the road last week, the Gophers surprised everybody and took the defending champs to overtime. Despite an offense that can't seem to get going, Minnesota has hung around in most games. I think we'll see something similar with the Gophers' defense limiting a UCLA offense that is somehow averaging fewer passing yards than Minnesota this season. The Bruins have a top-15 run game, though, so Minnesota's defense will have its hands full there. This is going to be the question going forward: until proven otherwise, can the Gophers' offense do just enough to squeak out a win? I'm predicting that, with the home crowd behind them, that's the case on Saturday.

#2770. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2769. Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick as Ireland seal emphatic victory over Argentina

Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as Ireland preserved their unbeaten home record against Argentina with a comfortable 42-12 bonus-point victory in the Nations Championship.

The Pumas had famously stunned Andy Farrell's 2025 British and Irish Lions squad on their previous visit to the Aviva Stadium, yet they entered the match having lost all 11 of their past meetings with Ireland in Dublin.

Felipe Contepomi's side took an early lead when Mateo Carreras caught a cross-field kick from Tomas Albornoz over diminutive scrum-half Craig Casey to touch down in the left corner.

However, full-back Keenan crossed the line either side of a try by captain Dan Sheehan, allowing the hosts to establish a 21-5 advantage by half-time.

Sam Prendergast registered his maiden international try alongside five successful conversions, before Keenan's third score and a powerful finish from Ronan Kelleher sealed a resounding win for the home team.

Carreras managed a late consolation try for Argentina, but the visitors' attempt to cause a surprise was hampered by yellow cards for Justo Piccardo and Efrain Elias, alongside an early head injury to skipper Julian Montoya.

This outcome was Ireland's third victory from four Nations Championship matches, following summer successes against Australia and Japan and a defeat to New Zealand.

With head coach Farrell accepting that his side must improve to compete at next year's World Cup, the opening fixture of the autumn provided an opportunity to assess several squad options.

Argentina's 10th-minute score further subdued a flat crowd which was significantly below capacity.

However, Ireland swiftly hit back. Casey initially won a turnover penalty and then started a flowing team move from right to left which culminated with Mack Hansen sending Keenan racing across the try line.

Ireland's win was a third from four matches in the Nations Championship after summer successes against Australia and Japan were followed by defeat against New Zealand (Getty)

Hooker Sheehan – captaining his country in the absence of the injured Caelan Doris – crashed over 10 minutes later after Nick Timoney was held up following a lineout maul.

Argentina lost hooker Montoya before falling further behind when Keenan collected another Hansen pass to dance past three defenders and powerfully pirouette over.

While the Pumas have a wretched record away to Ireland, they have won three of four World Cup meetings between the nations.

Their hopes of securing a landmark success on Irish soil were hampered further by centre Piccardo being sent to the sin bin in the 35th minute for not retreating following a penalty.

Sheehan was then denied his second try when he was forced into touch just before grounding in an incident which led to him and Montoya's replacement Leonel Oviedo each departing for head injury assessments.

Fly-half Prendergast secured Ireland's bonus point within two minutes of the restart, spotting a gap between Marcos Kremer and Juan Martin Gonzalez to superbly race away and dot down.

Keenan was unable to prevent Pumas wing Carreras scoring his second before completing his treble following quick hands from forwards Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and Ryan Baird.

Replacement hooker Kelleher then bulldozed over in the aftermath of Elias being sent to the bin for a high tackle on Keenan, with Ciaran Frawley converting.

Ireland prop Sam Illo – on for his home debut – became the third player shown a yellow card before Farrell's men cruised through the closing stages ahead of upcoming appointments with Fiji and world champions South Africa.

#2768. Broncos release S Taylor Rapp, but he will re-sign to the practice squad tomorrow

According to 9NEWS Denver's Mike Klis, the Denver Broncos released veteran safety Taylor Rapp. However, this is just a procedural move to open up a 53-man roster spot, and Rapp is expected to be signed back to the practice squad tomorrow and likely elevated to the game-day roster on Sunday.

With Pat Bryant expected to be activated off the injured reserve tomorrow, the team needed to open up a roster spot for their talented wide receiver.

With starting safety Brandon Jones ruled OUT and Talanoa Hufanga listed as questionable, it's possible we still see Rapp elevated to the game-day roster on Sunday. However, the Broncos also ruled out defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike and cornerback Kris Abrams-Draine, so they have some decisions to make when they announce which two players they are elevating from the practice squad tomorrow.

With Jones ruled out and Hufanga questionable, we likely see Rapp get the start on Sunday at one of the safety positions or at least see some significant playing time in the Broncos' secondary. Devon Key has seen some playing time while Hufanga and Jones have been sidelined, and JL Skinner made a strong case for some added playing time after his big hit on Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker at the goal line during the Broncos ' goal-line stand last Sunday. So, we will have to see how they distribute the playing time this Sunday vs. the Panthers.

Rapp's roster spot was needed for second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant, who is expected to be activated from the injured reserve tomorrow. Bryant will be a major boost to the Broncos' offense and will give quarterback Bo Nix yet another talented pass-catcher to target vs. the Panthers. This will also be Rapp's third practice squad elevation this season, so if they want to use him again after Sunday, they will need to re-sign him to the 53-man roster.

Stay tuned to Mile High Report tomorrow as we'll update you on Pat Bryant's likely activation from the injured reserve, and we'll have the practice squad elevation news for you as well.

#2767. Kristaps Porziņģis announces that he's stepping away from basketball

Friday afternoon, Golden State Warriors center Kristaps Porziņģis announced that he has decided to step away from basketball as he continues to address the autoimmune disorder postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) that has kept him off the court this season.

Traded to the Warriors at the February deadline, Porziņģis appeared in 15 games last season, averaging 16.1 points, 5.3 rebounds, 2.3 assists and 1.1 blocks in 23.7 minutes per appearance. Optimism that the 7-foot-3 center's health would cooperate led the two sides to agree to a two-year, $40 million deal in the summer.

Unfortunately, Porziņģis' case of POTS, which initially became an issue late in the 2024-25 season with the Celtics, flared up and has kept him from returning to the court.

On Wednesday, NBA insider Jake Fischer reported that the Warriors were withholding payment from Porziņģis and considered his absence unexcused. It was also reported that the team was looking to move him via trade, either immediately or after December 15, when most players will be trade-eligible.

Porziņģis said in his statement on Friday that he hopes to "work with (the Warriors) to find a solution that makes sense."

#2765. NFL news, live updates: Rams' Myles Garrett reportedly in line to return Sunday; Shedeur Sanders to start for Browns with Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol

We're officially into Week 9 of the NFL season (and the looming NFL trade deadline), where teams will have to make a decision on the intended course of the remainder of their season — are they going all in? Or is it time to tear it all down and look toward the future?

NFL fans also await news on the fate of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who has been touted as a potential trade-deadline mover as the Indianapolis Colts kicked off their franchise reset with a fire sale. They've already traded away two foundational players, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, for several draft picks as they look to the future, leaving us to wonder whether Taylor could be next.

The Los Angeles Rams could be a deadline buyer, as they've won back-to-back games and are reportedly already getting a long-awaited midseason reinforcement in the form of edge rusher Myles Garrett, a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and the league's single-season sack record holder.

Garrett's in line for a return to game action on the road Sunday against the Washington Commanders, according to NFL Network's Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport. Coming back from early-season knee surgery that landed him on injured reserve, Garrett has practiced all week.

Shedeur Sanders will start at quarterback for the Cleveland Browns in Week 9 against the New Orleans Saints, head coach Todd Monken announced.

Deshaun Watson returned to practice in a limited capacity on Friday, but remains in concussion protocol. Monken said it's unclear if Watson will serve as the backup this week, though he will be listed as questionable

The Browns' No. 1 quarterback took a helmet-to-helmet hit during the first quarter of Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Watson missed only four snaps, but later reported experiencing concussion symptoms on Monday night.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more ahead of Week 9.

The Seattle Seahawks sent a pair of draft picks to the Indianapolis Colts in exchange for six-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson.

After just one game in a Seahawks uniform, Nelson is now out.

He's "week-to-week," according to Seattle head coach Mike Macdonald, who told reporters Friday that the 30-year-old offensive lineman needs a minor knee procedure.

"We're not going to put him on IR," Macdonald said, via The Seattle Times' Bob Condotta.

When asked what happened to Nelson, Macdonald said the interior o-lineman had something he was dealing with when he arrived.

"We re-imaged it, and it was aggravated to some degree, so we've kind of done the due diligence, and everybody agrees it's best to take care of it now and play the long game."

Notably, the Seahawks will also be down quarterback Sam Darnold (quad) this week against the Arizona Cardinals. Backup Drew Lock will start in his place.

Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph is out for Week 9's matchup with the Miami Dolphins. However, Joseph took first-team reps as a limited participant in practice all week and "looked awesome," according to Lions safeties coach Jim O'Neil.

"The focus right now is let's see if we can stack some days," O'Neil told the Detroit Free Press' Dave Birkett. "Let's see if he can look like he looked yesterday for three or four days in a row."

Joseph, who turns 26 on Nov. 14, hasn't played for the Lions since Week 6 of last season due to a cartilage condition in his knee. He was an All-Pro selection in 2024, his third NFL season, compiling 9 interceptions and 83 tackles.

The Lions signed Joseph to a four-year extension in April 2025 that made him the highest-paid safety in the NFL at the time.

Injuries continue to plague the Eagles, who will again be without top receivers DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks this week against the Giants. The team has officially ruled out both wideouts for Sunday's game, after neither practiced on Friday.

Both Smith, who has been dealing with a hamstring injury, and Wicks, who has an ankle injury, have missed two games with the injury, and are set to now miss a third.

However, there's a bit of good news: Saquon Barkley, who was listed as limited in practice with hamstring and back injuries, should be clear to play on Sunday.

Kansas City Chiefs head coach Andy Reid told reporters Friday that rookies Peter Woods and Mansoor Delane won't play Sunday against the New York Jets.

"They're making progress, so that's a positive thing," Reid said of the defensive tackle and cornerback, per ESPN's Nate Taylor.

Woods is dealing with a neck injury, and Delane is navigating a shoulder issue. Delane, this year's No. 6 overall pick, hasn't played since a Week 7 loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Woods, whom the Chiefs selected 29th overall back in April, suffered his setback last week in a defeat to the Denver Broncos.

The New England Patriots have ruled out both wide receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) for Sunday's game against the Green Bay Packers.

They've listed tight end Hunter Henry — the team's receptions leader — as "questionable" with a foot issue.

Brown, whom the Patriots gave up a pair of picks for (including a 2028 first-rounder), has appeared in only three games this season. He suffered a high ankle sprain in the season opener and noted late last month that he wasn't 100 percent upon returning to game action.

As for Henderson, the second-year back revealed on Friday that he was hospitalized after experiencing "unexplained neurological symptoms."

Although the results of Henderson's examination were "positive and reassuring," doctors have yet to determine a cause, Henderson explained in his social media post.

Watson returned to practice in a limited capacity on Friday, but remains in concussion protocol. Monken said it's unclear if Watson will serve as the backup this week, though he will be listed as questionable

The Browns' No. 1 quarterback took a helmet-to-helmet hit during the first quarter of Sunday's loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Watson missed only four snaps, but later reported experiencing concussion symptoms on Monday night.

Los Angeles Rams edge rusher Myles Garrett is in line for a return to game action on the road Sunday against the Washington Commanders, according to NFL Network's Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport.

Garrett, coming back from early-season knee surgery that landed him on injured reserve, has practiced all week.

The two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year, who's also the league's single-season sack record holder, went under the knife in the wake of the Rams' season-opening defeat to the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne, Australia.

Watson entered concussion protocol earlier this week after reporting symptoms on symptoms on Monday night. Shedeur Sanders has worked with the first team to prepare in case Watson was ruled out.

Watson has not cleared concussion protocol yet, but is able to practice on a limited basis.

While the New York Jets will get Breece Hall back after a five-game absence following a quad injury, wide receiver Garrett Wilson is out for the team's road game against the Kansas City Chiefs.

Wilson entered concussion protocol after taking a hit to the head during last week's loss to the Las Vegas Raiders. He reported experiencing symptoms when he reported to the team's practice facility on Monday.

New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson released a statement on social media Friday explaining that his absence from the team is due to "unexplained neurological symptoms" that forced him to be hospitalized. Some of his "physical functions" have also been affected.

Henderson says he was examined, and while the results were "positive and reassuring," doctors have yet to determine a cause.

"Recently, I experienced an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days," Henderson wrote. "During that time, I underwent extensive medical testing and evaluation. While the results of my comprehensive medical testing have come back positive and reassuring, the cause of this remains unknown and unexplainable.

"I will continue working closely with specialists and physical therapists to focus on my recovery, as these symptoms have affected my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions. I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health. My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priorities."

The 24-year-old Henderson suffered a high ankle sprain in Week 4 and was initially expected to be out for multiple weeks. He did not miss a game as he played against the New York Jets and Chicago Bears, rushing for a total of 40 yards on 10 carries.

For the second straight day, the Patriots have designated wide receiver A.J. Brown and running back TreVeyon Henderson as DNP, leaving their offensive production in doubt ahead of Sunday's game against the Packers.

Brown, who returned from a high ankle sprain in Week 6, said last week that he's been "pushing through" the injury. He is listed as dealing with ankle and knee injuries.

TreVeyon Henderson is again listed as being out with an illness, though the team has not elaborated on his condition. Last month, Henderson was expected to be ruled out multiple weeks with a high ankle sprain, but continued playing for two more weeks before missing last week's game against the Dolphins.

#2762. Kristaps Porziņģis says he will 'step away' from basketball in wake of lingering health issues

Kristaps Porziņģis is stepping away from the NBA while dealing with ongoing health issues, the veteran center announced Friday.

In a statement on social media, Porziņģis said he was not able to play at the level he hoped and has decided to focus on his health.

"This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated," Porziņģis wrote. "I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love."

Porzingis, who signed a two-year, $40 million contract with the Golden State Warriors this summer, said he hopes to work with the Warriors to "find a solution that makes sense" going forward. The center has been indefinitely away from the team this season while dealing with his health.

ESPN reported Wednesday the Warriors have not paid Porzingis any of his $20 million annual salary while he contemplated his NBA future. Porzingis has reportedly not contested the lack of payments.

Porzingis was acquired by the Warriors before the trade deadline last February and signed the extension to stay in Golden State in June. However, a personal "health issue" caused him to miss the start of training camp.

Neither Porzingis nor the Warriors has clarified what the center has been dealing with. But Porzingis has been open about his struggles with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a chronic condition that can affect the nervous system. Last fall, Porzingis revealed his POTS symptoms flared up during the 2025 NBA playoffs, when he was with the Boston Celtics, and severely limited his ability to play.

Porzingis said last month he was "getting better and better" after consulting with doctors, though he called the health issues "frustrating." It is unclear if Friday's announcement is a full retirement, or just a pause in his NBA career.

Nicknamed "The Unicorn" for his unique big-man skillset, the 31-year-old Latvian center steps away from basketball after an 11-year career spread across six teams. Porzingis is a 2024 NBA champion with the Celtics and earned an All-Star nod in 2018.

#2760. WTA chair apologises to Pegula for airing of 'diva' comment

Women's Tennis Association chair Valerie Camillo has apologised to Jessica Pegula and said the live-streaming of private comments to her coach about fellow player Mirra Andreeva was "regrettable and unacceptable".

American Pegula called Andreeva a "diva" in a private conversation with her coach after a practice session for the WTA Tour Finals on Wednesday.

However, the comments were aired on a live stream after the WTA failed to tell players there were microphones on practice courts.

Camillo said that all audio recording equipment in practice areas had since been removed as "clearly there was a failure in our technical execution and monitoring".

"I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles," she added.

"What happened was regrettable and unacceptable. Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction."

WTA takes responsibility after Pegula 'diva' comment live-streamed

Pegula was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and her coach Conchita Martinez encourages her behaviour.

A representative for Pegula said she had been in direct contact with those involved and had been "completely unaware" the conversation could be heard by courtside microphones.

None of the players were asked about the incident in the pre-tournament news conference at Indian Wells on Friday, but Pegula did address it in an interview with ESPN.

"I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance and audio and access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past," she said.

"I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, [the] last couple of years really, where it just seems highly unnecessary.

At the same major, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek said players were being watched "like animals in the zoo" by behind-the-scenes cameras.

YouTube streams of Wednesday's practice sessions at Indian Wells have since been removed by the WTA, but the footage had already been shared on social media.

"There was a lack of advanced notice and clear signage to assist players about the recording equipment operating in the area."

#2757. Warriors' Kristaps Porzingis issues update on his health, NBA future

Golden State Warriors center Kristaps Porziņģis, who has not been with the team as he addresses long-term health concerns, announced he will step away from basketball.

"This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated," Porziņģis wrote Friday, Nov. 6 in a statement posted to social media.

"I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love."

It's worth noting that Porziņģis didn't outright mention retirement in the statement, which could potentially leave a return to the sport down the road, should his health improve.

Porziņģis, 31, has been dealing with an undisclosed illness that has prevented him from joining the Warriors. He had missed all of training camp in late September and has been away from the team. Warriors coach Steve Kerr said last month that Porziņģis would be in the team facility for a check-in with Golden State's sports medicine and performance team.

Previously, stretching back to Porziņģis' final season with the Celtics in 2024-25, he had expressed frustrations over repeated absences that were caused from an undiagnosed condition that prevented him from having the energy and stamina to play.

Eventually, Porziņģis disclosed that he was dealing with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) autoimmune symptoms, though he has not offered specific updates in recent months.

The Celtics traded Porziņģis to the Hawks in June 2025. Just eight months later, Atlanta then shipped Porziņģis in a separate deal to the Warriors, where he played only 15 games for the team.

ESPN reported Wednesday, Nov. 4 that Porziņģis was not being paid his $20 million salary for failing to render services to the team.

A one-time All-Star, Porziņģis is known for stretching the floor with his shooting range, while providing a rim-protecting presence on the other end. Across his 10-year career, Porziņģis has averaged 19.5 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.9 assists per game in 533 appearances.

"In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense," Porziņģis continued in his statement. "I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support. Onwards and upwards."

#2752. Kristaps Porzingis Is “Stepping Away” From The NBA: Shocking End To 10-Year Career

At just 31 years old, 10-year veteran Kristaps Porzingis should be in the prime of his career. Certainly, when he signed that two-year contract with the Golden State Warriors back in June, he never imagined having to step away just five months later.

Nevertheless, Porzingis could no longer deny his current reality, which is why he's calling it quits (for now). In a shocking and emotional statement on social media, Porzingis revealed his status and explained the decision to put his career on hold.

"This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated," wrote Porzingis in a statement. "I'm doing good, but I know what it takes, and I'm not where I want to be to perform at the level that I expect from myself. At this point, I've made the decision to prioritize my health and step away from the game I love. In this situation, I want to show the utmost respect for the Golden State Warriors and work with them to find a solution that makes sense. I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support."

With averages of 16.7 points, 5.2 rebounds, 2.5 assists, 0.6 steals, and 1.2 blocks per game on 44.6% shooting in 2025-26, you can't entirely blame the Warriors for thinking Porzingis was ready to play a big role this season. On paper, he's the perfect floor spacer for Steph Curry and fills a position they've been lacking for years. Even so, there were signs that his health was unreliable.

For starters, there's his extensive injury history, which is enough by itself to cast serious doubt on his availability. Since his rookie year with the Knicks, Porzingis has only played 60 or more games in a season twice. There's also the fact that he agreed to a two-year deal this summer, with just $3 million guaranteed in 2027-28. If that was the best he could do, it likely means he was acutely aware of his own uncertain future.

Regardless of what Porzingis expected, it's a tragic and unfortunate turn for what was once such a promising career. Drafted fourth overall in 2015, the Knicks saw his potential, even if the fans didn't. Slowly but surely, he proved the team right, validating their pick by rising into a star.

In his third season, however, Porzingis' career experienced its first major setback with an ACL injury that kept him out for the entire following season. He came back as a Dallas Maverick, but his game was never the same again. Over the years, as he tried different roles on various teams, he was only ever able to show glimpses of his star potential before some injury would derail his progress.

Now, his time with the Warriors, and possibly in the NBA itself, has come to an end with practically nothing to show for it. As Porzingis prioritizes his health and seeks treatment from doctors, it's the Warriors who will have to adjust. Whether it's a simple buyout or a trade agreement, they are open to all options when it comes to turning Porzingis' contract into someone who can contribute now, and what they do next could determine their trajectory for many years to come.
